before.label: AI operating costs
before.title: An agent’s design is becoming part of its price
before.author: Codex
before.teaser: Context length, generated output and search calls can activate different charges. The same task can carry a different bill depending on how the agent attempts it.
before.summary: Microsoft prices fixed-choice decisions without an output-token charge. Anthropic raises Haiku’s rates above a prompt-length threshold. DeepSeek meters search and page retrieval separately, while Google’s Argon discount expires on a set date. These terms make workflow structure and timing part of the bill, before any change in the task’s objective.
before.meaning: The prices create incentives to design work differently. A routing decision may only need a choice among options; an accumulating conversation can enter a higher price tier; repeated searches add a per-call meter. A system that becomes more persistent or remembers more may therefore change its economics without changing its listed model. Promotions introduce another jump when the same workflow starts paying the normal rate. These are billing mechanisms, not measured savings between equivalent systems or a calculation of human-inclusive cost.
before.watch: Watch how bills change as conversations grow, how often agents repeat paid tool calls, and whether specialized steps preserve the needed quality. DeepSeek’s integration waiver ends October 31 at 16:00 UTC; Argon’s introductory rates end November 30.

before.timelineIntro: The releases put different meters around the same broad activity of getting work done. Comparing the headline token rate alone misses those architectural and calendar effects.

developments.title: DeepSeek prices search and page retrieval separately
developments.text: Search and Fetch each cost $0.75 per 1,000 API calls. For DeepSeek API users, calls through server-side tools in DeepSeek Harness, Claude Code and Codex are temporarily free; billing for those integrations starts October 31 at 16:00 UTC. The waiver does not cover every direct API call.
developments.relation: Separately priced search and retrieval calls directly extend the briefing’s analysis of total task cost and expiring promotions.

developments.title: Google sets a time-limited Argon price
developments.text: Argon’s public model launches at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. Google lists $4 and $20 respectively after the introductory period expires November 30, 2026.

developments.title: Microsoft prices fixed-choice decisions
developments.text: Decision-1 scores predefined options for tasks such as routing and classification. Microsoft lists $0.042 per million input tokens and no output-token charge. This is a different output from a general-purpose model’s written answer.

developments.title: Anthropic ties Haiku prices to prompt length
developments.text: For prompts up to 100,000 tokens, Haiku 5.5 input costs $0.10 and output $0.50 per million tokens. Above that threshold, the rates are $0.50 and $2.50 respectively; cached input has separate pricing.

after.label: AI operating costs
after.title: An agent’s design is becoming part of its price
after.author: Codex
after.teaser: The cost of a longer conversation depends on both the provider's meter and the model's memory design. Cheaper serving only improves the economics if the agent still recalls what the task requires.
after.summary: Microsoft prices fixed-choice decisions without an output-token charge. Anthropic raises Haiku’s rates above a prompt-length threshold. DeepSeek meters search and page retrieval separately, while Google’s Argon discount expires on a set date. These terms make workflow structure and timing part of the bill, before any change in the task’s objective.
after.meaning: The prices create incentives to design work differently. A routing decision may only need a choice among options; an accumulating conversation can enter a higher price tier; repeated searches add a per-call meter. AWS and i14 now describe a different constraint: Laplace 3B compresses history into fixed-size serving state. That could let a provider serve longer-running agents without growing each conversation's state as its history lengthens. Compression still has to preserve the information the task needs. Our inference is that this shifts part of the cost question from how much history to keep toward how reliably it remains usable. These are potential serving benefits, not measured savings for equivalent completed tasks or a promise of lower customer prices.
after.watch: Watch retrieval quality as histories grow, customer bills versus provider serving cost, and repeated paid tool calls. Fixed serving state is not lossless recall or fixed total system memory. DeepSeek’s integration waiver ends October 31 at 16:00 UTC; Argon’s introductory rates end November 30.

after.timelineIntro: Earlier releases changed the bill through output choices, context thresholds and tool charges. The new AWS/i14 case concerns the underlying cost of serving history. Provider costs and customer prices can move differently.

developments.title: A fixed-state model changes the memory constraint
developments.text: AWS and i14 report 29.5 MB of recurrent state per sequence for Laplace 3B, independent of context length. History is compressed, and retrieval quality needs workload-specific evaluation.
developments.relation: New architecture evidence distinguishes the provider's serving constraints from the customer-facing billing mechanisms already tracked.

added.label: AI chip competition
added.title: Rival AI chips need to become cheap to try
added.author: Codex
added.teaser: A lower chip price is hard to act on when testing it requires a rewrite. Familiar software can make another supplier a credible option before a buyer moves its largest workload.
added.summary: Google has opened TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend that it says runs existing workloads with minimal code changes. Separately, AWS and i14 describe adapting a custom model to Trainium2 through native PyTorch. That project still required specialized engineering. Together, they show two different hurdles: making another chip accessible to developers and making a real workload run well on it.
added.meaning: An alternative supplier has little leverage if evaluating its offer is itself a major project. Shared tools can lower that initial cost while preserving developers' existing skills. Our inference is that this creates a purchasing option before it creates a production migration: buyers can test a rival's offer without first replacing their whole workflow. The advantage may then shift toward the supplier that makes representative trials easiest to reproduce. Compatibility alone cannot establish which hardware delivers the better result for the money.
added.watch: Watch engineering hours needed for a representative trial, performance under real traffic and the work required to operate it afterward. Compare equivalent models and quality. A familiar interface can lower the cost of evaluation without eliminating specialized optimization or ongoing cloud dependence.
added.visualTitle: How another supplier becomes a real option
visual: Reduce the work needed to start a trial
Compare offers before committing to a move
added.timelineIntro: These October 20 sources describe separate developments: Google's general-purpose backend and an AWS/i14 implementation case. The case study tests the limits of the broader promise; it is not a head-to-head chip comparison.

developments.title: Google brings native PyTorch to TPUs
developments.text: Google releases a native PyTorch backend for its chips. Its primary announcement qualifies migration as requiring minimal code changes.
developments.relation: Directly checked Google announcement establishes a familiar developer interface as a route to testing another hardware supplier.

developments.title: A Trainium2 case exposes the remaining engineering
developments.text: AWS and i14 describe changes to kernels, communication and compilation. A fixed-batch test also concealed delays under changing traffic.
developments.relation: A distinct native-PyTorch implementation demonstrates why framework compatibility and useful workload performance are separate tests.
